entries.meaning: To beg someone urgently and humbly for something; formal and literary in modern American English.
examples: The families beseech the governor to reopen the case.
Her lawyers besought the judge for one more week.
Advocates have besought the agency for years to publish the data.
The pilgrims besought heaven for rain.
He had besought his father to forgive him before the old man died.
In the last chapter she beseeches the reader to remember her kindly.

senses.head: Beg urgently, implore
body: Formal and literary; in ordinary speech Americans beg or plead instead. The regular past beseeched is now more common in American writing than besought. (умолять, упрашивать)
examples: The families beseech the governor to reopen the case.
Her lawyers besought the judge for one more week.
Advocates have besought the agency for years to publish the data.

senses.head: Entreat in prayer or older prose
body: The scriptural and literary register, where besought is the expected past. You meet it in translations, hymns, and historical fiction rather than in speech. (молить, взывать)
examples: The pilgrims besought heaven for rain.
He had besought his father to forgive him before the old man died.
In the last chapter she beseeches the reader to remember her kindly.

entries.register: formal — literary and scriptural; in ordinary speech Americans beg or plead
entries.contrast: The regular beseeched is now the more common past in American writing; besought is literary and turns up mainly in older prose and translations of scripture. Either is correct, so long as you use the same one twice: ✗ he beseeched them, and had besought them again.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of asking, so it reports a speech act rather than a state. No linking or stative use.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is the person begged, and it is obligatory: the families beseech the governor, ✗ the families beseech. Usually completed by an infinitive (beseech him to forgive her) or by for + the thing wanted (besought the judge for one more week).
entries.passive: yes, though formal like the verb itself — the judge was besought for one more week; the agency has been besought for years to publish the data.

entries.meaning: To carry or take someone or something to the place where you are or are going; also, to cause a result or a state.
examples: Please bring your ID to the appointment.
She brought dessert to the potluck.
Somebody has brought a dog into the lobby.
Spring brings the tourists back.
The merger brought three years of chaos.
That decision has brought nothing but lawsuits.
It took a strike to bring about a new contract.
Their reporting brought about the resignation.
Technology has brought about changes nobody planned for.
Don't bring up the layoffs at dinner.
She brought up the budget again.
Nobody has brought it up since the meeting.
He was brought up by his grandmother.
They brought up four kids on one salary.
She has brought up two children alone.
The store brings in about six thousand a week.
They brought in a consultant after the second outage.
We have brought in two new engineers this quarter.
The scandal brought down the mayor.
Nothing will bring down a fever that fast.
Generic drugs have brought prices down sharply.
I can't bring myself to sell the house.
She never brought herself to apologize.
He has never brought himself to watch the tape.
Prosecutors may still bring charges.
The tenants brought a class action.
The state has brought three cases against the company.

senses.head: Carry or take to this place
body: The motion is toward the speaker or toward the place being talked about. If the movement is away from you, the verb is take. (приносить, приводить, привозить)
examples: Please bring your ID to the appointment.
She brought dessert to the potluck.
Somebody has brought a dog into the lobby.

senses.head: Cause a state or result
body: The subject produces the effect, and the object is usually abstract: rain, joy, trouble, publicity, change. (приносить, вызывать, приводить к)
examples: Spring brings the tourists back.
The merger brought three years of chaos.
That decision has brought nothing but lawsuits.

senses.head: Bring about (cause to happen)
body: A fixed phrase for making a change actually happen, often after effort or delay. (осуществить, вызвать, привести к)
examples: It took a strike to bring about a new contract.
Their reporting brought about the resignation.
Technology has brought about changes nobody planned for.

senses.head: Bring up (raise a topic)
body: To introduce a subject into a conversation, often one others would rather avoid. (поднять тему, упомянуть)
examples: Don't bring up the layoffs at dinner.
She brought up the budget again.
Nobody has brought it up since the meeting.

senses.head: Bring up (raise a child)
body: Common in both countries, though Americans often prefer raise. Frequently passive: he was brought up in Ohio. (воспитывать, растить)
examples: He was brought up by his grandmother.
They brought up four kids on one salary.
She has brought up two children alone.

senses.head: Bring in (earn or recruit)
body: Two everyday uses: money that a business takes in, and a person hired or called in from outside. (приносить доход; привлекать со стороны)
examples: The store brings in about six thousand a week.
They brought in a consultant after the second outage.
We have brought in two new engineers this quarter.

senses.head: Bring down (topple or reduce)
body: Used both of removing someone from power and of lowering a number such as a price, a fever, or a rate. (свергнуть; сбить, снизить)
examples: The scandal brought down the mayor.
Nothing will bring down a fever that fast.
Generic drugs have brought prices down sharply.

senses.head: Bring oneself to (force oneself)
body: Almost always negative or with can't: you are unable to make yourself do something painful. (заставить себя)
examples: I can't bring myself to sell the house.
She never brought herself to apologize.
He has never brought himself to watch the tape.

senses.head: Bring charges, bring a suit
body: The standard legal collocation for starting a case against someone. (выдвинуть обвинения, подать иск)
examples: Prosecutors may still bring charges.
The tenants brought a class action.
The state has brought three cases against the company.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: ✗ brang and ✗ brung are heard in some American dialects but are never standard. The trap is that sing/sang/sung and ring/rang/rung look like they should set the pattern; bring refuses to join them. Also keep brought (carried) apart from bought (paid for).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, from carrying (bring your ID) to causing (spring brings the tourists back). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and freely ditransitive: bring me the file, bring her a chair. The object is obligatory — ✗ she brought is incomplete. The particle uses keep the object (bring up the layoffs, bring in a consultant).
entries.passive: yes, and very common — he was brought up by his grandmother; three cases have been brought against the company; the resignation was brought about by their reporting.
entries.phrasal verbs: bring about · bring along · bring around · bring back · bring down · bring forward · bring in · bring off · bring on · bring out · bring to · bring up

entries.meaning: To get something by paying money for it; informally, also to believe something or to gain it at a cost.
examples: We buy our vegetables at the farmers market.
He bought the truck used, with ninety thousand miles on it.
They have bought a house outside Tucson.
I don't buy that excuse.
The jury never bought his story.
Nobody has bought that line since the first press conference.
The delay bought us two more weeks.
A second server would buy some breathing room.
That concession has bought them nothing at all.
You cannot buy a federal judge.
The company bought off two inspectors.
Someone had bought his silence long before the hearing.
Half the team never bought into the new process.
She bought into the partnership in 2019.
Investors have bought into the story completely.
His brothers bought him out.
They offered to buy her out at book value.
A private equity firm has bought out the chain.

senses.head: Purchase, pay money for
body: The core sense. Keep it apart from brought, the past of bring: money makes it bought. (покупать, приобретать)
examples: We buy our vegetables at the farmers market.
He bought the truck used, with ninety thousand miles on it.
They have bought a house outside Tucson.

senses.head: Believe, accept as true
body: Informal, and usually negative: I don't buy it. The object is a story, an excuse, or an argument. (верить, купиться на)
examples: I don't buy that excuse.
The jury never bought his story.
Nobody has bought that line since the first press conference.

senses.head: Gain at a cost
body: What is paid is not always money; the object is often time, silence, safety, or goodwill. (выиграть (время), купить ценой чего-либо)
examples: The delay bought us two more weeks.
A second server would buy some breathing room.
That concession has bought them nothing at all.

senses.head: Bribe, buy off
body: Informal but unambiguous. With off it means paying someone to drop an objection or a claim. (подкупить)
examples: You cannot buy a federal judge.
The company bought off two inspectors.
Someone had bought his silence long before the hearing.

senses.head: Buy into (accept, or take a stake)
body: Either to be persuaded by an idea or to purchase a share of a business. The context separates them. (принять идею; войти в долю)
examples: Half the team never bought into the new process.
She bought into the partnership in 2019.
Investors have bought into the story completely.

senses.head: Buy out (purchase someone's share)
body: To acquire the whole of another party's stake so they leave the business. (выкупить долю)
examples: His brothers bought him out.
They offered to buy her out at book value.
A private equity firm has bought out the chain.

entries.register: everyday — the ordinary word for paying money for something
entries.contrast: Bought and brought are one letter apart and are swapped constantly: ✗ I brought a new laptop when you mean you paid for one. If money changed hands it is bought; if you carried it somewhere it is brought.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the purchase, bribery, and buy out senses. The believe sense (I don't buy it) is mental but still takes the progressive: I'm not buying that story.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and ditransitive in buy her a coffee, buy us two more weeks. The object is normally obligatory (✗ we bought at the market), though buy can stand alone in shopping contexts: we buy local.
entries.passive: yes — the truck was bought used; two inspectors were bought off; the chain has been bought out by a private equity firm.
entries.phrasal verbs: buy back · buy in · buy into · buy off · buy out · buy up

entries.meaning: To take hold of something moving, and by extension to capture, reach in time, notice, or contract something.
examples: Dogs catch frisbees better than most people do.
She caught the glass before it hit the floor.
The goalie has caught everything they have thrown at him.
Traps rarely catch anything this time of year.
We caught three fish and threw them all back.
Police have caught the driver.
He caught his roommate going through his mail.
Don't let them catch you parking there.
Two managers have been caught falsifying the logs.
If I run I can catch the 6:40.
She caught the last train out of the city.
We have caught that flight twice with ten minutes to spare.
Kids catch everything in their first year of school.
He caught a cold the week before the wedding.
She has caught the flu twice this winter.
I didn't catch your last name.
He caught only half of what she said over the noise.
Nobody has caught the joke yet.
Spellcheck catches the obvious ones.
She caught the discrepancy on the second read.
An intern has caught two errors the auditors missed.
The zipper catches about halfway up.
My sleeve caught on the door handle.
A branch had caught the kite ten feet up.
Go ahead; I'll catch up.
He caught up on email over the weekend.
We have caught up on the backlog at last.
The name never caught on.
She caught on faster than anyone expected.
The style has caught on with younger buyers.

senses.head: Seize something moving
body: The literal sense: stop an object in flight with your hands. (ловить, поймать)
examples: Dogs catch frisbees better than most people do.
She caught the glass before it hit the floor.
The goalie has caught everything they have thrown at him.

senses.head: Capture, trap
body: Of animals, fish, or people who are running from you. (поймать, задержать)
examples: Traps rarely catch anything this time of year.
We caught three fish and threw them all back.
Police have caught the driver.

senses.head: Discover someone in the act
body: Normally catch someone doing something, with an -ing form and never an infinitive. (застать, поймать с поличным)
examples: He caught his roommate going through his mail.
Don't let them catch you parking there.
Two managers have been caught falsifying the logs.

senses.head: Be in time for
body: Of trains, flights, the end of a movie, or a person before they leave. (успеть на, застать)
examples: If I run I can catch the 6:40.
She caught the last train out of the city.
We have caught that flight twice with ten minutes to spare.

senses.head: Contract an illness
body: Used of infections you pick up from other people, not of chronic conditions. (подхватить, заразиться)
examples: Kids catch everything in their first year of school.
He caught a cold the week before the wedding.
She has caught the flu twice this winter.

senses.head: Hear or understand
body: Usually negative or in an apology: I didn't catch that. (расслышать, уловить)
examples: I didn't catch your last name.
He caught only half of what she said over the noise.
Nobody has caught the joke yet.

senses.head: Notice, spot a mistake
body: Of errors, discrepancies, and problems found before they do damage. (заметить, обнаружить)
examples: Spellcheck catches the obvious ones.
She caught the discrepancy on the second read.
An intern has caught two errors the auditors missed.

senses.head: Snag, become stuck
body: The subject is the thing that snags, and the phrase is normally catch on something. (зацепиться, застрять)
examples: The zipper catches about halfway up.
My sleeve caught on the door handle.
A branch had caught the kite ten feet up.

senses.head: Catch up (reach the same point)
body: Of distance, of work left undone, or of news between friends who have not talked in a while. (догнать, наверстать)
examples: Go ahead; I'll catch up.
He caught up on email over the weekend.
We have caught up on the backlog at last.

senses.head: Catch on (become popular; understand)
body: Two settled meanings: a fashion or a name spreads, or a person finally grasps what is going on. (прижиться, войти в моду; сообразить)
examples: The name never caught on.
She caught on faster than anyone expected.
The style has caught on with younger buyers.

entries.register: everyday — constant in speech, from catching a ball to catching a cold
entries.contrast: ✗ catched is not a form. For the many Americans with the cot–caught merger, caught /kɔt/ and cot /kɑt/ sound identical, but the spelling never wavers — and caught is spelled with the same -aught as taught.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, including the involuntary ones (catch a cold, catch the joke). No linking or stative use.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in most senses (caught the glass, caught three fish), intransitive in the zipper catches and in catch on / catch up (go ahead; I'll catch up).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the driver has been caught; two managers have been caught falsifying the logs. Restricted for the illness sense, where the active is the only natural form: ✗ a cold was caught by him.
entries.phrasal verbs: catch at · catch on · catch out · catch up · catch up on · catch up with

entries.meaning: To move slowly, quietly, and low to the ground, or to advance by small degrees.
examples: Don't creep around behind me like that.
The cat crept along the fence rail.
He had crept downstairs before anyone else woke.
Doubt creeps in around three in the morning.
A little sarcasm crept into her emails.
Costs have crept up about four percent this year.
Ivy will creep up the north wall if you let it.
Moss crept over the stones.
The vine has crept across the whole trellis.
Winter crept up on us.
She creeps up on you with the sad part of the song.
The deadline has crept up on everyone.
That mask creeps me out.
The whole basement creeped us out.
His messages have creeped her out for weeks.

senses.head: Move slowly and stealthily
body: Quiet movement meant to go unnoticed, often close to the ground. (красться, ползти)
examples: Don't creep around behind me like that.
The cat crept along the fence rail.
He had crept downstairs before anyone else woke.

senses.head: Advance by small degrees
body: Figurative, usually with up or in: costs, delays, doubts, and errors creep rather than jump. (расти незаметно, вкрадываться)
examples: Doubt creeps in around three in the morning.
A little sarcasm crept into her emails.
Costs have crept up about four percent this year.

senses.head: Grow along a surface
body: Of ivy, vines, and moss; the adjective creeping names whole plant families. (стелиться, виться (о растениях))
examples: Ivy will creep up the north wall if you let it.
Moss crept over the stones.
The vine has crept across the whole trellis.

senses.head: Creep up on (approach unnoticed)
body: Of a person sneaking up, and just as often of a date or a season arriving before you noticed. (подкрасться незаметно)
examples: Winter crept up on us.
She creeps up on you with the sad part of the song.
The deadline has crept up on everyone.

senses.head: Creep someone out
body: Informal, and the one use of this verb with a regular past: that movie creeped me out, never crept me out. (жутко пугать, вызывать мурашки)
examples: That mask creeps me out.
The whole basement creeped us out.
His messages have creeped her out for weeks.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary in speech, especially in creep out and creep up on
entries.contrast: The past is crept — except in the fixed slang phrase creep someone out, which is regular: that movie creeped me out, ✗ that movie crept me out.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and typically slow or gradual: literal movement (the cat crept along the fence) and figurative advance (costs have crept up).
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every literal and figurative sense — the direction is carried by a preposition (creep along the rail, creep into her emails). Transitive only in the fixed slang creep someone out.
entries.passive: no for the movement senses, which have no object at all: ✗ the fence rail was crept along. The one passive is the slang idiom — I was completely creeped out by that mask.
entries.phrasal verbs: creep in · creep out · creep up · creep up on

entries.meaning: To let your mind wander to pleasant imaginary things while you are awake.
examples: I daydream through most of the Monday status call.
He daydreamed his way through an hour of the lecture.
My son has daydreamed through two years of algebra.
I daydream about a week with no phone.
She daydreamed about quitting for the whole drive home.
They have daydreamed about opening a bakery for years.

senses.head: Drift off, stop paying attention
body: No object: the point is the lapse of attention rather than what you imagine. American English uses daydreamed; daydreamt reads as British. (витать в облаках, отвлекаться)
examples: I daydream through most of the Monday status call.
He daydreamed his way through an hour of the lecture.
My son has daydreamed through two years of algebra.

senses.head: Daydream about (imagine what you want)
body: With about or of. What follows is a wish rather than a plan, which is what separates it from plan or intend. (мечтать, грезить о чём-либо)
examples: I daydream about a week with no phone.
She daydreamed about quitting for the whole drive home.
They have daydreamed about opening a bakery for years.

entries.register: everyday — the ordinary word for letting your mind wander
entries.pattern: regular -ed in American English (British ea → e + t)
entries.contrast: Built on dream, so it takes the same two pasts — but the split is even sharper here. American writing uses daydreamed almost without exception; daydreamt, which the spreadsheet lists, reads as British or deliberately old-fashioned. See dream.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it names an ongoing mental activity and takes the progressive freely: he was daydreaming through the lecture.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no object at all; what is imagined goes into a prepositional phrase with about or of: I daydream about a week with no phone, ✗ I daydream a week with no phone.
entries.passive: no — there is no object to promote: ✗ a bakery was daydreamed about for years is not how this is said. Only the awkward prepositional passive is even conceivable, and Americans avoid it.

entries.meaning: To handle or cope with something, to hand out playing cards, or to trade in goods.
examples: I deal with vendor complaints all morning.
He dealt with the same landlord for six years.
The agency has dealt with worse crises than this one.
Deal me in.
She dealt the cards and we started playing.
The house has dealt him four bad hands in a row.
The shop deals in rare maps.
His family dealt in grain for a century.
They have dealt in used equipment since the eighties.
You do not deal on that corner without permission.
Two of them dealt out of the same apartment.
She has never dealt anything harder than weed.
Judges deal out the same sentence for both offenses.
The ruling dealt a blow to the plaintiffs.
Life has dealt him a bad hand this year.
Chapter four deals with the war years.
The report dealt with only one of the three sites.
Nobody has dealt with the legal side in print.

senses.head: Deal with (handle, cope with)
body: The everyday sense, always with with. The object is a problem, a complaint, or a difficult person. (справляться, иметь дело с)
examples: I deal with vendor complaints all morning.
He dealt with the same landlord for six years.
The agency has dealt with worse crises than this one.

senses.head: Hand out playing cards
body: The card-table sense, and the source of the noun dealer and of a raw deal. (сдавать карты)
examples: Deal me in.
She dealt the cards and we started playing.
The house has dealt him four bad hands in a row.

senses.head: Deal in (trade in, sell)
body: Of a business and the goods it handles. Also figurative: a paper that deals in rumor. (торговать чем-либо)
examples: The shop deals in rare maps.
His family dealt in grain for a century.
They have dealt in used equipment since the eighties.

senses.head: Sell illegal drugs
body: Informal, and usually with no object at all: he got caught dealing. (торговать наркотиками)
examples: You do not deal on that corner without permission.
Two of them dealt out of the same apartment.
She has never dealt anything harder than weed.

senses.head: Deal a blow, deal out
body: Somewhat formal. The object is a blow, damage, justice, or the hand that fate gives you. (нанести удар; раздавать, воздавать)
examples: Judges deal out the same sentence for both offenses.
The ruling dealt a blow to the plaintiffs.
Life has dealt him a bad hand this year.

senses.head: Deal with (be about)
body: Of books, chapters, reports, and laws: what the text covers. (быть посвящённым, рассматривать тему)
examples: Chapter four deals with the war years.
The report dealt with only one of the three sites.
Nobody has dealt with the legal side in print.

entries.register: everyday — deal with it and deal the cards are both plain speech
entries.contrast: The spelling keeps the ea but the vowel shortens: dealt rhymes with belt, not with sealed. ✗ dealed is not a form, and ✗ delt is a common misspelling.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses. The be about use (chapter four deals with the war years) is closer to a state but still takes the ordinary tenses, not the progressive: ✗ chapter four is dealing with the war years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive and ditransitive in deal me in, deal him four bad hands, dealt the plaintiffs a blow; prepositional-intransitive in deal with and deal in; bare intransitive in the drug sense (he got caught dealing).
entries.passive: yes — the cards were dealt; a blow was dealt to the plaintiffs. The prepositional passive is natural too: the complaint has already been dealt with.
entries.phrasal verbs: deal in · deal out · deal with · deal with, deal in

entries.meaning: To see images and stories while asleep, or to imagine something you badly want.
examples: I rarely dream about work.
She dreamed about her grandmother's house again.
He has dreamed the same thing three nights running.
We dream of a year with no travel.
She dreamed of medical school and got there.
He has dreamed of playing at Carnegie Hall since he was six.
I wouldn't dream of asking her to pay.
She never dreamed it would take four years.
Nobody had dreamed the vote would be that close.
Marketing dreams up a new slogan every quarter.
Who dreamed this policy up?
We had dreamed up the whole plan over one dinner.
A corner office in year one? Dream on.
He thinks they'll double the offer. Dream on.

senses.head: See images while asleep
body: With about or of. English makes the sleeper the subject, so Russian мне снилось becomes I dreamed. American English writes dreamed; dreamt is British and sounds poetic here. (видеть сон, сниться)
examples: I rarely dream about work.
She dreamed about her grandmother's house again.
He has dreamed the same thing three nights running.

senses.head: Wish for, aspire to
body: With of or about, and often with since or always to show how long the wish has lasted. (мечтать о)
examples: We dream of a year with no travel.
She dreamed of medical school and got there.
He has dreamed of playing at Carnegie Hall since he was six.

senses.head: Imagine as possible
body: Almost always negative: never dreamed, wouldn't dream of it. The second is also a polite refusal. (и представить себе (не мог))
examples: I wouldn't dream of asking her to pay.
She never dreamed it would take four years.
Nobody had dreamed the vote would be that close.

senses.head: Dream up (invent)
body: Of a plan, a name, or an excuse, usually with a hint that it was invented too quickly. (выдумать, придумать)
examples: Marketing dreams up a new slogan every quarter.
Who dreamed this policy up?
We had dreamed up the whole plan over one dinner.

senses.head: Dream on (informal dismissal)
body: A fixed imperative used to tell someone their hope is unrealistic. It appears in no other form. (мечтать не вредно, размечтался)
examples: A corner office in year one? Dream on.
He thinks they'll double the offer. Dream on.

entries.register: everyday — used constantly in speech and writing alike
entries.pattern: regular -ed in American English (British ea → e + t)
entries.contrast: Both forms are correct, but they split by country: dreamed is the ordinary American past and participle, while dreamt /drɛmt/ is the British default and sounds poetic in American prose. The same split gives British leant, learnt, spelt, and burnt where Americans write leaned, learned, spelled, and burned.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it names an activity or an experience over time and takes the progressive: she was dreaming about the house again. No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — normally intransitive with about or of (I dream of a year with no travel), transitive with a content object (he has dreamed the same thing three nights running) and in dream up a slogan.
entries.passive: restricted — natural only for dream up: the whole plan was dreamed up over one dinner. The ordinary senses have no passive: ✗ her grandmother's house was dreamed about.
entries.phrasal verbs: dream about, dream of · dream of · dream on · dream up

entries.meaning: To experience an emotion or a sensation, to touch something to learn about it, or to hold an impression or an opinion.
examples: I feel better after a walk.
They felt ignored by management for months.
He has felt dizzy since the medication changed.
Feel how heavy this is.
She felt the fabric and put it back on the shelf.
The doctor has felt the swelling and ordered a scan.
Can you feel the draft from that window?
We felt the tremor an hour before the news reported it.
I have not felt my toes since mile eight.
The room feels colder than the thermostat says.
The whole meeting felt rehearsed.
This draft has felt wrong from page one.
I feel we should wait a week.
She felt the price was too high.
The board has felt that way since the audit.
I feel like pizza.
Nobody felt like driving another three hours.
She has not felt like going out since the move.
I feel for anyone flying today.
We all felt for him after the news.
She has felt for those families from the start.
Do you feel up to a walk?
He didn't feel up to the drive.
She has not felt up to company all week.
Feel them out before you name a number.
We felt out two other vendors.
He has already felt out the committee.

senses.head: Experience an emotion or state
body: Followed by an adjective, not an adverb: I feel bad, not the adverb form. (чувствовать себя, испытывать)
examples: I feel better after a walk.
They felt ignored by management for months.
He has felt dizzy since the medication changed.

senses.head: Touch to examine
body: Deliberate touching to find out about texture, temperature, or swelling. (щупать, трогать)
examples: Feel how heavy this is.
She felt the fabric and put it back on the shelf.
The doctor has felt the swelling and ordered a scan.

senses.head: Perceive by sensation
body: Here the stimulus comes from outside you: wind, a bump, a tremor, pain. (ощущать, почувствовать)
examples: Can you feel the draft from that window?
We felt the tremor an hour before the news reported it.
I have not felt my toes since mile eight.

senses.head: Seem, give an impression
body: The subject is a thing or a place rather than a person, and it takes an adjective: the room feels cold. (казаться, ощущаться)
examples: The room feels colder than the thermostat says.
The whole meeting felt rehearsed.
This draft has felt wrong from page one.

senses.head: Hold an opinion
body: Softer than think: a judgment offered as personal rather than argued. (считать, полагать)
examples: I feel we should wait a week.
She felt the price was too high.
The board has felt that way since the audit.

senses.head: Feel like (want, be in the mood for)
body: Followed by a noun or an -ing form, never an infinitive: feel like leaving, not feel like to leave. (хотеться)
examples: I feel like pizza.
Nobody felt like driving another three hours.
She has not felt like going out since the move.

senses.head: Feel for (sympathize with)
body: Fellow feeling for someone in trouble. Do not confuse it with feel up, which is something else entirely. (сочувствовать)
examples: I feel for anyone flying today.
We all felt for him after the news.
She has felt for those families from the start.

senses.head: Feel up to (be well enough for)
body: Mostly in questions and negatives, about energy or health rather than ability. (быть в состоянии, чувствовать в себе силы)
examples: Do you feel up to a walk?
He didn't feel up to the drive.
She has not felt up to company all week.

senses.head: Feel out (probe cautiously)
body: To test someone's position quietly before committing to a proposal. (прощупать почву)
examples: Feel them out before you name a number.
We felt out two other vendors.
He has already felt out the committee.

entries.register: everyday — among the most frequent verbs in the language
entries.contrast: ✗ feeled does not exist. Felt is also an everyday noun — the fabric in a felt hat — spelled and pronounced the same; only the sentence tells them apart.
entries.verb type: stative in the emotion and opinion senses (I feel better, I feel we should wait) — the opinion sense refuses the progressive: ✗ I am feeling we should wait. Linking (copular) in the room feels cold, the meeting felt rehearsed. Action only in the deliberate senses: feel the fabric, feel them out.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the linking use (this draft has felt wrong), transitive in felt the fabric, felt the tremor, and with a that-clause in the opinion sense. Feel like takes a noun or an -ing form, never an infinitive: ✗ feel like to leave.
entries.passive: restricted — fine where the act is deliberate or the sensation is shared: the swelling was felt and a scan ordered; the tremor was felt across three counties; the committee has already been felt out. No passive of the linking use (✗ cold is felt by the room) or of the opinion sense (✗ the price was felt too high by her).
entries.phrasal verbs: feel for · feel like · feel out · feel up · feel up to

entries.meaning: To go on having something, to store it somewhere, or to make someone or something stay in a state.
examples: Keep the change.
He kept every letter she sent him.
They have kept the same phone number since 1998.
We keep the extra keys in the kitchen drawer.
She kept the deed in a safe-deposit box.
The store has kept my measurements on file.
Keep the door open.
The noise kept us awake.
That heater has kept the shop warm all winter.
My landlord keeps raising the rent.
He kept apologizing until it got awkward.
She has kept asking the same question for a month.
He keeps his promises.
She kept the news to herself all week.
They have not kept a single appointment this month.
They keep chickens and two goats.
He kept a family of five on a machinist's wage.
The parish has kept records since 1830.
Hard cheese keeps for months.
The soup kept fine in the freezer.
Whatever it is has kept this long, so it can wait until Monday.
I can't keep up with the reading.
He kept up with the leaders for ten miles.
They have kept up the payments without a single miss.
Keep him from signing anything today.
She kept herself from laughing.
The tarp has kept the rain off the woodpile.
Keep to the schedule.
We kept to the main road.
He has kept to the same routine for twenty years.

senses.head: Continue to have, retain
body: The opposite of giving something back or throwing it away. (оставлять себе, сохранять)
examples: Keep the change.
He kept every letter she sent him.
They have kept the same phone number since 1998.

senses.head: Store in a place
body: Where a thing lives when it is not in use; usually with a place phrase. (хранить, держать)
examples: We keep the extra keys in the kitchen drawer.
She kept the deed in a safe-deposit box.
The store has kept my measurements on file.

senses.head: Cause to stay in a state
body: Takes an object plus an adjective, a participle, or a place: keep the door open, keep them waiting. (держать, поддерживать в каком-либо состоянии)
examples: Keep the door open.
The noise kept us awake.
That heater has kept the shop warm all winter.

senses.head: Keep doing (continue)
body: Always with an -ing form, never an infinitive: keep trying, not keep to try. Keep on is the emphatic version. (продолжать делать, всё время делать)
examples: My landlord keeps raising the rent.
He kept apologizing until it got awkward.
She has kept asking the same question for a month.

senses.head: Observe, fulfill, hold to
body: The object is a promise, an appointment, a secret, a schedule, or a law. (сдержать, соблюдать, хранить (тайну))
examples: He keeps his promises.
She kept the news to herself all week.
They have not kept a single appointment this month.

senses.head: Look after, support, maintain
body: Of animals, gardens, records, or a household you pay for. This is the sense behind earn your keep. (содержать, ухаживать за, вести (записи))
examples: They keep chickens and two goats.
He kept a family of five on a machinist's wage.
The parish has kept records since 1830.

senses.head: Stay fresh, last
body: No object, and mostly of food. Figuratively, news that will keep can wait until later. (храниться, не портиться)
examples: Hard cheese keeps for months.
The soup kept fine in the freezer.
Whatever it is has kept this long, so it can wait until Monday.

senses.head: Keep up (maintain a pace or standard)
body: Either matching someone else's speed or continuing something at the same level. (успевать, поддерживать на прежнем уровне)
examples: I can't keep up with the reading.
He kept up with the leaders for ten miles.
They have kept up the payments without a single miss.

senses.head: Keep from, keep off (prevent)
body: Keep someone from doing something is preventing it; keep off keeps a thing away. (удерживать, не давать, уберечь)
examples: Keep him from signing anything today.
She kept herself from laughing.
The tarp has kept the rain off the woodpile.

senses.head: Keep to (stick to, stay within)
body: Of a schedule, a route, a budget, or a routine. Keep to yourself is a separate fixed phrase meaning to stay private. (придерживаться, держаться)
examples: Keep to the schedule.
We kept to the main road.
He has kept to the same routine for twenty years.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: ✗ keeped is not a form — the long ee shortens to kept /kɛpt/, rhyming with slept and crept. What follows keep is an -ing form, never an infinitive: keep trying, ✗ keep to try. The noun keep (earn your keep, the castle keep) is spelled the same and has no past at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but several senses describe maintaining a state rather than a single act (keep the shop warm, keep asking). The resultative pattern keep the door open is complex-transitive, not linking: the adjective describes the object, not the subject.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in most senses, and complex-transitive with an added adjective, participle, or place (keep them waiting, keep the keys in the drawer). Intransitive in the freshness sense: hard cheese keeps for months. Keep + -ing only: keep trying, ✗ keep to try.
entries.passive: yes — every letter she sent him was kept; records have been kept since 1830; we were kept awake by the noise. No passive of the intransitive sense: ✗ for months is kept by hard cheese.
entries.phrasal verbs: keep at · keep away · keep back · keep down · keep from · keep in · keep off · keep on · keep out · keep to · keep up · keep up with · keep up with, catch up with, catch up on

entries.meaning: To go down on your knees, or to stay in that position.
examples: You have to kneel to see the bottom shelf.
He knelt to tie his son's shoe.
She has knelt on that hard floor for an hour.
The ushers ask the congregation to kneel at that point in the service.
The pilgrims knelt on the stone steps.
They have knelt there every evening since the accident.
Athletes still kneel at some events.
Several players kneeled during the anthem.
Half the team had kneeled before the anthem even started.

senses.head: Go down on your knees
body: Both pasts are standard American English: knelt is usual in edited prose, kneeled in sports and news writing. The k is silent in every form. (опуститься на колени, встать на колени)
examples: You have to kneel to see the bottom shelf.
He knelt to tie his son's shoe.
She has knelt on that hard floor for an hour.

senses.head: Kneel in prayer or reverence
body: The religious use, where knelt is strongly preferred. (преклонить колени, молиться на коленях)
examples: The ushers ask the congregation to kneel at that point in the service.
The pilgrims knelt on the stone steps.
They have knelt there every evening since the accident.

senses.head: Take a knee in protest
body: A recent American use dating from the 2016 anthem protests; kneeled is the past you usually see in this context. (встать на одно колено в знак протеста)
examples: Athletes still kneel at some events.
Several players kneeled during the anthem.
Half the team had kneeled before the anthem even started.

entries.register: everyday — the ordinary verb for going down on one's knees
entries.contrast: Both pasts are standard American English. Knelt is the more common in edited prose; kneeled shows up especially in sports and news writing (he kneeled during the anthem). The k is silent in every form — /nil/, /nɛlt/, never ✗ /knil/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it covers both the movement down (he knelt to tie his son's shoe) and staying in the position (she has knelt there for an hour).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — never takes an object: ✗ she knelt the floor. Purpose or place is added by a phrase (kneel on the stone steps, kneel to see the bottom shelf).
entries.passive: no — an intransitive verb has nothing to promote to subject: ✗ the stone steps were knelt on by the pilgrims is at best strained, and the protest sense has no passive at all.

entries.meaning: To bend or rest your body or an object at an angle, and by extension to tend toward a position or rely on someone.
examples: Don't lean out that far.
He leaned over the counter to read the sign.
She has leaned into the aisle to see the screen all game.
The old barn leans about two degrees to the east.
She had leaned her bike against the wrong tree.
The fence has leaned toward the road since the storm.
The county leans Republican.
I leaned toward the cheaper option.
The committee has leaned that way from the start.
You can lean on me for the deposit.
His brother leaned on him to sell.
We have leaned on that one vendor too much this quarter.
We should lean in rather than apologize.
The brand leaned in on the joke.
They have leaned in hard on video this year.

senses.head: Bend the body from upright
body: Movement of your own body toward or away from something. American English uses leaned; leant is British and a homophone of lent. (наклоняться)
examples: Don't lean out that far.
He leaned over the counter to read the sign.
She has leaned into the aisle to see the screen all game.

senses.head: Rest against a support
body: Of a person or an object propped at an angle; also of a structure that has tilted and stayed that way. (прислонять, опираться)
examples: The old barn leans about two degrees to the east.
She had leaned her bike against the wrong tree.
The fence has leaned toward the road since the storm.

senses.head: Tend toward, be inclined
body: With toward, or with left and right when the subject is a voter, a county, or a paper. (склоняться к)
examples: The county leans Republican.
I leaned toward the cheaper option.
The committee has leaned that way from the start.

senses.head: Lean on (rely on, or pressure)
body: Two meanings held apart by context: depending on someone for support, or, informally, coercing them. (полагаться на; давить на, нажимать)
examples: You can lean on me for the deposit.
His brother leaned on him to sell.
We have leaned on that one vendor too much this quarter.

senses.head: Lean in (commit, engage fully)
body: Business slang of the last decade: to embrace something instead of hedging or apologizing for it. (активно включиться, не отступать)
examples: We should lean in rather than apologize.
The brand leaned in on the joke.
They have leaned in hard on video this year.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary in speech; only the British past leant is marked
entries.pattern: regular -ed in American English (British ea → e + t)
entries.contrast: Leaned is the American past and participle. Leant /lɛnt/, the form the spreadsheet lists, is British — and it is a homophone of lent, the past of lend, which is one good reason American writing leaves it alone.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the body senses (he leaned over the counter). Closer to stative where it reports a standing tilt or tendency: the old barn leans two degrees east, the county leans Republican.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in most senses (don't lean out that far, I leaned toward the cheaper option), transitive when you prop something: she had leaned her bike against the wrong tree.
entries.passive: restricted — possible only in the propping sense: the ladder was leaned against the wall. No passive of the tendency or posture senses (✗ toward the cheaper option was leaned), though the prepositional passive works for pressure: he was leaned on to sell.

entries.meaning: To jump a long way or high, and by extension to rise sharply or to act suddenly.
examples: Deer leap that fence every spring.
The cat leapt from the counter to the top of the fridge.
He had leapt out of the way just in time.
Rents leap every time a new building opens.
The stock leapt again on no real news.
Sales have leaped thirty percent since March.
Don't leap into a lease you can't break.
She leaped at the chance to transfer.
He has leaped at every opening they have posted.
She leaps to conclusions faster than anyone I know.
The press leapt to the obvious conclusion.
We have leaped to the wrong one twice already.

senses.head: Jump far or high
body: Both leaped /lipt/ and leapt /lɛpt/ are standard American, unlike dreamt and leant. (прыгать, скакать)
examples: Deer leap that fence every spring.
The cat leapt from the counter to the top of the fridge.
He had leapt out of the way just in time.

senses.head: Rise sharply (of numbers)
body: Of prices, sales, rents, or stock, and always a sudden move rather than a steady climb. (резко подскочить, взлететь)
examples: Rents leap every time a new building opens.
The stock leapt again on no real news.
Sales have leaped thirty percent since March.

senses.head: Leap at (act eagerly)
body: Of an offer or a chance taken without hesitation. Leap into something carries a warning about haste. (ухватиться за, броситься)
examples: Don't leap into a lease you can't break.
She leaped at the chance to transfer.
He has leaped at every opening they have posted.

senses.head: Leap to conclusions
body: A fixed phrase, always a criticism: judging before the facts are in. (делать поспешные выводы)
examples: She leaps to conclusions faster than anyone I know.
The press leapt to the obvious conclusion.
We have leaped to the wrong one twice already.

entries.forms: leap /lip/ · leaped /lipt/ or leapt /lɛpt/ · leaped /lipt/ or leapt /lɛpt/
entries.register: neutral — at home in writing and in fixed phrases (leap year, leap of faith); plain speech says jump
entries.contrast: Unlike dreamt and leant, leapt is fully at home in American English. Leaped is somewhat more common in edited American prose, but leapt is standard and frequent in narrative. Note that they are pronounced differently: leaped /lipt/ keeps the long vowel, leapt /lɛpt/ shortens it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and always a sudden move rather than a gradual one, literally (deer leap that fence) or of numbers (the stock leapt again).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the destination or obstacle comes with a preposition (leapt from the counter, leaped at the chance). What looks like an object in leap that fence is a path phrase, not a true object.
entries.passive: no — there is no object to promote: ✗ the chance was leaped at by her is not idiomatic, and ✗ conclusions are leapt to survives only as a set phrase.

entries.meaning: To go away from a place or a person, or to let something stay behind or stay in a condition.
examples: We leave for the airport at six.
They left before the second act.
The train leaves from track nine.
Half the staff will leave if that policy stands.
She left him in the spring.
He has left the company after eleven years.
Don't leave your laptop in the car.
She left her badge on her desk.
I have left you three voicemails.
Leave the light on.
The news left everyone speechless.
The flood has left two blocks without power.
People rarely leave anything to a second cousin.
Her aunt left her the cabin.
He has left everything to the university.
Leave it to me.
They left the wording to the lawyers.
We have left the scheduling up to her.
There are two cookies left.
Six from ten leaves four.
Nothing was left of the barn but the foundation.
Leave the middle section out.
You left out the best part.
They have left two names out of the credits.
Leave her alone.
The team left him behind in free agency.
Growth has left the older neighborhoods behind.

senses.head: Go away, depart
body: With or without an object: leave the house, leave for Chicago, or simply leave. (уходить, уезжать, отправляться)
examples: We leave for the airport at six.
They left before the second act.
The train leaves from track nine.

senses.head: Quit for good
body: Of a job, a school, a band, or a marriage, where the departure is permanent. (уйти с работы, бросить (кого-либо))
examples: Half the staff will leave if that policy stands.
She left him in the spring.
He has left the company after eleven years.

senses.head: Let something stay behind
body: Covers both deliberate leaving and simple forgetting; a message left for someone belongs here too. (оставить, забыть где-либо)
examples: Don't leave your laptop in the car.
She left her badge on her desk.
I have left you three voicemails.

senses.head: Cause to remain in a state
body: Takes an object plus an adjective or a participle: leave the door open, left us speechless. (оставить в каком-либо состоянии)
examples: Leave the light on.
The news left everyone speechless.
The flood has left two blocks without power.

senses.head: Bequeath
body: Of property passed on at death, usually with an indirect object: left her the cabin. (завещать, оставить в наследство)
examples: People rarely leave anything to a second cousin.
Her aunt left her the cabin.
He has left everything to the university.

senses.head: Entrust, delegate
body: Leave it to me, or leave something up to someone: handing over responsibility for a decision. (предоставить, поручить)
examples: Leave it to me.
They left the wording to the lawyers.
We have left the scheduling up to her.

senses.head: Remain, be left over
body: Normally the participle with be, and the standard way to state a remainder in arithmetic. (оставаться в остатке)
examples: There are two cookies left.
Six from ten leaves four.
Nothing was left of the barn but the foundation.

senses.head: Leave out (omit)
body: Of information or people left off a list, whether by accident or on purpose. (пропустить, не включить)
examples: Leave the middle section out.
You left out the best part.
They have left two names out of the credits.

senses.head: Leave alone, leave behind
body: Leave alone means stop bothering; leave behind means abandon or outpace. (оставить в покое; оставить позади)
examples: Leave her alone.
The team left him behind in free agency.
Growth has left the older neighborhoods behind.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: ✗ leaved is not a verb form; it exists only inside compounds like broad-leaved. Left doubles as the direction and as an adjective meaning remaining (two cookies left), all spelled the same.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, from departing (we leave at six) to bequeathing (her aunt left her the cabin). The resultative leave the door open is complex-transitive, not linking.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in they left before the second act, transitive in don't leave your laptop in the car, and ditransitive in left her the cabin, I have left you three voicemails.
entries.passive: yes, and constant — two blocks have been left without power; two names were left out of the credits; nothing was left of the barn but the foundation. Note that left in two cookies left is an adjective, not a passive.
entries.phrasal verbs: leave aside · leave behind · leave off · leave out · leave over

entries.meaning: To stop having something, to be unable to find it, or to fail to win.
examples: I lose my glasses about twice a day.
She lost her keys somewhere between the car and the door.
He had lost the receipt, so the store refused the return.
That team loses whenever it rains.
We lost the game in overtime.
They have lost four straight.
You lose the signal in that tunnel.
He lost his job in the second round of cuts.
She has lost twenty pounds since January.
Nobody wants to lose a parent that young.
She lost her father last spring.
The town has lost three people to that road.
Try not to lose your nerve at the last minute.
He lost his temper in the meeting.
I have lost track of how many times we have filed this.
Every delay loses money.
We lost an hour to a bad merge.
The project has lost two months to review.
Lose the jacket; it's ninety degrees.
He lost them somewhere in the parking garage.
She has lost the accent almost completely.
We got lost twice on the way up.
You lost me at the second slide.
He has lost me completely with this explanation.

senses.head: Misplace, be unable to find
body: Spelling trap: lose has one o and ends in /z/; loose is the adjective meaning not tight. (терять, потерять)
examples: I lose my glasses about twice a day.
She lost her keys somewhere between the car and the door.
He had lost the receipt, so the store refused the return.

senses.head: Fail to win
body: Of games, elections, bets, and court cases. You lose to an opponent and lose by a margin. (проигрывать)
examples: That team loses whenever it rains.
We lost the game in overtime.
They have lost four straight.

senses.head: Cease to have
body: Of a job, weight, hair, a signal, or a reputation: something you had that is now gone. (лишиться, утратить)
examples: You lose the signal in that tunnel.
He lost his job in the second round of cuts.
She has lost twenty pounds since January.

senses.head: Be bereaved of
body: The ordinary English way of saying someone died: she lost her father. Plain, not euphemistic. (потерять близкого человека)
examples: Nobody wants to lose a parent that young.
She lost her father last spring.
The town has lost three people to that road.

senses.head: Fail to keep control of
body: With control, your temper, track, patience, your nerve: things that slip away rather than get misplaced. (потерять контроль, самообладание)
examples: Try not to lose your nerve at the last minute.
He lost his temper in the meeting.
I have lost track of how many times we have filed this.

senses.head: Waste, fail to use
body: Of time, money, and opportunities consumed with nothing to show for them. (терять время, упускать возможность)
examples: Every delay loses money.
We lost an hour to a bad merge.
The project has lost two months to review.

senses.head: Get rid of, shake off
body: Informal: lose a pursuer, or lose something unwanted such as a jacket or an attitude. (отделаться, оторваться от преследования)
examples: Lose the jacket; it's ninety degrees.
He lost them somewhere in the parking garage.
She has lost the accent almost completely.

senses.head: Be lost (astray, or not following)
body: The participle behaves like an adjective, so I am lost is a state, not a past tense. It covers both losing your way and losing the thread of an explanation. (заблудиться; не понимать)
examples: We got lost twice on the way up.
You lost me at the second slide.
He has lost me completely with this explanation.

entries.register: everyday — constant in speech, about games, keys, and jobs alike
entries.contrast: Three traps in one word. Spelling: lose (one o, a verb) is not loose (two o's, an adjective meaning not tight). Sound: lose ends in /z/, loose in /s/. And lost is both the past and a common adjective — I am lost is not a past tense at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, though most senses report a change of state the subject did not choose (he lost his job, she lost her father). Lost in I am lost is an adjective, not a tense.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in nearly every sense (lost her keys, lost his temper), intransitive in the competition sense: that team loses whenever it rains.
entries.passive: yes — the game was lost in overtime; the receipt had been lost; two months have been lost to review. The bereavement sense resists it: ✗ her father was lost by her is not how this is said.
entries.phrasal verbs: lose out · lose out on · lose out to

entries.meaning: A modal verb expressing possibility or permission; might is its past form and also a weaker present possibility.
examples: The delay may push the launch to April.
She might come, but I doubt it.
The road might be closed by then.
He might have taken the earlier flight.
The package may have gone to the old address.
We may have met at a conference years ago.
You may leave once the form is signed.
May I ask who's calling?
Students may not retake the exam.
She said we might need a second interview.
He told the class they might use their notes.
The letter said applicants may appeal within thirty days.
You might want to call ahead.
We might as well start without him.
She might try the other entrance.
It may be legal, but it is a terrible idea.
He may have the votes; he does not have the money.
The design may look odd at first, and then it makes sense.
May you both be very happy.
May it please the court.

senses.head: Express possibility
body: May states a real chance, might a slighter one. No -s, no -ing, and no to after either. (может быть, возможно)
examples: The delay may push the launch to April.
She might come, but I doubt it.
The road might be closed by then.

senses.head: May have, might have (past possibility)
body: To place a possibility in the past, use may have or might have plus a participle. There is no participle of may itself, so have might does not exist. (возможно, сделал что-либо)
examples: He might have taken the earlier flight.
The package may have gone to the old address.
We may have met at a conference years ago.

senses.head: Grant or ask permission
body: Formal register. In everyday American speech people use can; may survives in rules, notices, and polite questions. (можно, разрешается)
examples: You may leave once the form is signed.
May I ask who's calling?
Students may not retake the exam.

senses.head: Might in reported speech
body: This is where might still works as a true past: it is the backshifted form of may after a past reporting verb. (мог, можно было (в косвенной речи))
examples: She said we might need a second interview.
He told the class they might use their notes.
The letter said applicants may appeal within thirty days.

senses.head: Might as a tentative suggestion
body: A softened recommendation, usually you might want to or might as well. Only the might form works this way. (пожалуй, стоило бы)
examples: You might want to call ahead.
We might as well start without him.
She might try the other entrance.

senses.head: Concede a point
body: Formal. May grants something before the sentence turns on it, normally with but. (пусть и, хотя и)
examples: It may be legal, but it is a terrible idea.
He may have the votes; he does not have the money.
The design may look odd at first, and then it makes sense.

senses.head: Formal wish
body: Ceremonial and literary, with may at the front of the clause and no subject inversion elsewhere. (пусть, да будет)
examples: May you both be very happy.
May it please the court.

entries.register: everyday — a core modal, though might now carries most of its weight in speech
entries.third person: no -s form — ✗ he mays · -ing form: no -ing form — ✗ maying
entries.contrast: May is a modal, so it breaks nearly every rule in this file: no -s, no -ing, no to after it, and no real participle — ✗ I have might. Might is the historical past and still works that way in reported speech (She said we might need a second interview), but in modern American English it mostly stands on its own as a weaker present-tense possibility: She may come (a real chance) versus She might come (less likely). To talk about a past possibility, use may have or might have plus a participle.
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — never a main verb. It has no -s form (✗ he mays), no -ing form (✗ maying), and no participle (✗ I have might); might is its past, used for backshift (she said we might need a second interview) and as a weaker present possibility.
entries.transitivity: Neither — a modal takes no object. It is followed by a bare infinitive, never by to: you may leave, ✗ you may to leave. Past possibility uses may have / might have plus a participle.
entries.passive: no — a modal has no passive of its own: ✗ permission was mayed. It combines freely with a passive infinitive, which is a different thing: the form may be signed once it is witnessed.

entries.meaning: To have a particular sense, to intend something, or to matter to someone.
examples: What does this abbreviation mean?
The red light meant the door was locked.
That symbol has meant the same thing since the 1950s.
I don't mean to interrupt.
I meant to call you back yesterday.
We have meant to repaint this room for years.
What I mean is that we can't ship on Friday.
She had meant it as a compliment.
He has never meant anything by it.
A second round means another two weeks.
The merger meant layoffs in both offices.
That change has meant rewriting half the tests.
Your opinion means more to him than you think.
The award meant nothing to her.
That has meant a great deal to my family.
This chair was meant for the hallway.
You are meant to sign both copies.
They were meant for each other.

senses.head: Signify, denote
body: What a word, a sign, or a gesture stands for. The subject is the thing that carries the sense. (означать, значить)
examples: What does this abbreviation mean?
The red light meant the door was locked.
That symbol has meant the same thing since the 1950s.

senses.head: Intend to do
body: Followed by an infinitive. I meant to usually introduces an apology for not doing it. (намереваться, собираться)
examples: I don't mean to interrupt.
I meant to call you back yesterday.
We have meant to repaint this room for years.

senses.head: Intend a particular sense
body: About the speaker's intent rather than the words: what you were trying to say or to do by saying it. (иметь в виду)
examples: What I mean is that we can't ship on Friday.
She had meant it as a compliment.
He has never meant anything by it.

senses.head: Entail, result in
body: The subject is an event or a decision and the object is its consequence. (означать (последствие), влечь за собой)
examples: A second round means another two weeks.
The merger meant layoffs in both offices.
That change has meant rewriting half the tests.

senses.head: Matter, have value to someone
body: Always with to someone, and usually with a quantity: means a lot, means nothing. (значить, быть важным для кого-либо)
examples: Your opinion means more to him than you think.
The award meant nothing to her.
That has meant a great deal to my family.

senses.head: Be meant for, be meant to
body: Passive only. Be meant for is purpose or destiny; be meant to states what the rules or instructions require. (быть предназначенным, полагаться)
examples: This chair was meant for the hallway.
You are meant to sign both copies.
They were meant for each other.

entries.register: everyday — used constantly, from what do you mean to I meant to call
entries.contrast: Meant is spelled with ea but rhymes with sent — /mɛnt/, not ✗ /mint/ — which is why learners write ✗ ment. ✗ meaned is not a form.
entries.verb type: stative in the core senses — signify (that symbol means the same thing), entail (a second round means another two weeks), and matter (your opinion means more to him). All refuse the progressive: ✗ that symbol is meaning. Action only in the intention sense: I meant to call you back.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object may be a noun (meant nothing to her), a that-clause (what I mean is that we can't ship), or an infinitive (I don't mean to interrupt). The object is obligatory: ✗ the red light meant is incomplete.
entries.passive: no in the stative senses — this is one learners get wrong: ✗ the same thing is meant by that symbol, ✗ a great deal has been meant to my family by that. The only passive is the fixed be meant for / be meant to (you are meant to sign both copies, they were meant for each other), which has no matching active.

entries.meaning: To beat someone by thinking more cleverly than they do.
examples: You can't outthink a machine at chess anymore.
Their defense outthought ours for four quarters.
She has outthought every negotiator they have sent.
He outthought himself and passed on the obvious answer.
We have outthought ourselves on this design.

senses.head: Outsmart, outmaneuver mentally
body: A prefixed think, inflecting exactly like it. Common in sports, chess, and negotiation. (перехитрить, переиграть умом)
examples: You can't outthink a machine at chess anymore.
Their defense outthought ours for four quarters.
She has outthought every negotiator they have sent.

senses.head: Outthink oneself
body: Reflexive and always a criticism: you lose by choosing the clever answer over the obvious one. (перемудрить, перехитрить самого себя)
examples: He outthought himself and passed on the obvious answer.
We have outthought ourselves on this design.

entries.register: rare — a prefixed think, met mostly in sports and strategy writing
entries.contrast: A prefixed think, so it inflects exactly like its base — see think. Watch the spelling: out + think keeps both t's, giving outthink and outthought.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, inflecting exactly like its base think, but only in the competitive sense: to beat someone mentally. No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — ✗ their defense outthought is incomplete. The object is a person or a side, or a reflexive in the self-defeating sense: he outthought himself.
entries.passive: yes — our defense was outthought for four quarters; every negotiator they have sent has been outthought. The reflexive use has no passive, as expected.

entries.meaning: To sleep longer than you meant to.
examples: If I oversleep, start the meeting without me.
He overslept and missed his connection.
She has overslept twice this week.
They had overslept, so breakfast was already cleared away.
My roommate oversleeps every single Monday.

senses.head: Sleep past the time you meant to get up
body: No object: you simply oversleep, never oversleep your alarm. It always implies the sleep was accidental, which is what separates it from sleep in. (проспать, заспаться)
examples: If I oversleep, start the meeting without me.
He overslept and missed his connection.
She has overslept twice this week.
They had overslept, so breakfast was already cleared away.
My roommate oversleeps every single Monday.

entries.register: everyday — prefixed, but the ordinary word for missing your alarm
entries.contrast: A prefixed sleep, inflecting the same way — see sleep. It takes no object: you simply oversleep, ✗ oversleep your alarm.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and always accidental, which is what separates it from the deliberate sleep in.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — takes no object at all: if I oversleep, start without me, ✗ I overslept my alarm. What was missed goes in a separate clause: he overslept and missed his connection.
entries.passive: no — an objectless intransitive has no passive: ✗ the alarm was overslept.

entries.meaning: To think about something again in order to change your plan or your opinion.
examples: We should rethink the launch date.
She had rethought her answer by the time she reached the door.
I have rethought my position on remote work.
Every startup rethinks its pricing in year two.
The board rethought the whole budget in one afternoon.
They have rethought their return policy twice this year.

senses.head: Reconsider a decision
body: Of one choice, date, or answer, held up for a second look. (пересмотреть решение, передумать)
examples: We should rethink the launch date.
She had rethought her answer by the time she reached the door.
I have rethought my position on remote work.

senses.head: Redesign an approach
body: Of a system, a policy, or a business model rather than a single decision. The noun shifts its stress to the first syllable: the plan needs a rethink. (переосмыслить, перестроить подход)
examples: Every startup rethinks its pricing in year two.
The board rethought the whole budget in one afternoon.
They have rethought their return policy twice this year.

entries.register: neutral — common in news and workplace speech, rarer in casual talk
entries.contrast: A prefixed think and inflects with it — see think. The stress moves when it becomes a noun: the verb is /ˌriˈθɪŋk/, the noun /ˈriθɪŋk/ (the plan needs a rethink).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a prefixed think used only in the deliberate sense of reconsidering, so it lacks think's stative opinion use.
entries.transitivity: transitive in normal use — we should rethink the launch date, rethought the whole budget. The object can be left out when it is obvious from context (the board may have to rethink), but it is usually present.
entries.passive: yes — the whole budget was rethought in one afternoon; the return policy has been rethought twice this year.

entries.meaning: To try to find or obtain something; formal in American English, where everyday speech says look for.
examples: Applicants may seek an extension in writing.
The company sought damages in federal court.
He had sought asylum twice before.
Birds seek open water in a hard freeze.
Rescuers sought the hikers for three days.
Investigators have sought those records since May.
The paper seeks comment from both sides before publishing.
We sought a second opinion.
She has sought advice from three different lawyers.
The bill seeks to close that loophole.
The administration sought to limit the damage.
Plaintiffs have sought to reopen the case twice.
New employees should seek out a mentor.
He sought out the one person who had read the file.
She has sought out every recording he ever made.
She is the most sought-after editor in town.
Those are the most sought-after seats in the building.

senses.head: Try to obtain
body: The commonest American use, and mostly legal or official: you seek damages, asylum, a permit, approval, or office. (добиваться, искать (чего-либо))
examples: Applicants may seek an extension in writing.
The company sought damages in federal court.
He had sought asylum twice before.

senses.head: Try to find, search for
body: Formal or literary. In speech Americans look for their keys and seek only records, evidence, or shelter. (искать, разыскивать)
examples: Birds seek open water in a hard freeze.
Rescuers sought the hikers for three days.
Investigators have sought those records since May.

senses.head: Ask for advice or comment
body: The object is what you request from another person: advice, comment, a second opinion, guidance. (обращаться за, запрашивать)
examples: The paper seeks comment from both sides before publishing.
We sought a second opinion.
She has sought advice from three different lawyers.

senses.head: Seek to do (attempt)
body: Formal written English with an infinitive. The plain equivalent is try to. (стремиться, пытаться)
examples: The bill seeks to close that loophole.
The administration sought to limit the damage.
Plaintiffs have sought to reopen the case twice.

senses.head: Seek out (go and find deliberately)
body: The particle adds effort and intent: you go looking for one specific person or thing. (разыскать, отыскать)
examples: New employees should seek out a mentor.
He sought out the one person who had read the file.
She has sought out every recording he ever made.

senses.head: Sought-after (in demand)
body: Only an adjective, built on the participle and normally placed before the noun. (востребованный, желанный)
examples: She is the most sought-after editor in town.
Those are the most sought-after seats in the building.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing and news; in speech Americans look for things
entries.contrast: Formal — in ordinary American speech you look for things and seek only damages, asylum, comment, or advice. Keep the r straight in American pronunciation: sought /sɔt/ has no r, sort /sɔrt/ does.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and formal in American English, where speech prefers look for. No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is what you want (sought damages, seeks comment), and it is obligatory: ✗ rescuers sought for three days needs the hikers. It also takes an infinitive: the bill seeks to close that loophole.
entries.passive: yes, and idiomatic in official prose — damages were sought in federal court; comment has been sought from both sides. The participle has also hardened into an adjective: the most sought-after editor in town.

entries.meaning: To rest with your eyes closed and your mind unconscious.
examples: I sleep badly in hotels.
The baby slept through the whole flight.
He has slept on that couch for a month.
The cabin sleeps six.
That rental slept eight comfortably.
The van has slept three of us on longer trips.
We sleep in on Sundays.
She slept in until noon.
I have not slept in since the baby came.
Sleep on it and tell me tomorrow.
They slept on the offer and countered Monday.
We have slept on worse decisions than this one.
Everyone assumed they had slept together.
She slept with his best friend and told him herself.
Half the plot turns on who sleeps with whom.
Sleep it off and call me in the morning.
He slept off the jet lag on the couch.
She has slept off worse hangovers than that.

senses.head: Rest unconscious
body: No object in this sense: I slept badly, not I slept a bad night. (спать)
examples: I sleep badly in hotels.
The baby slept through the whole flight.
He has slept on that couch for a month.

senses.head: Provide beds for
body: The subject is a house, a boat, a tent, or a van, and the object is a number of people. (вмещать (о числе спальных мест))
examples: The cabin sleeps six.
That rental slept eight comfortably.
The van has slept three of us on longer trips.

senses.head: Sleep in (stay in bed late)
body: Deliberate and pleasant, which is exactly what separates it from oversleep. (поспать подольше, залежаться)
examples: We sleep in on Sundays.
She slept in until noon.
I have not slept in since the baby came.

senses.head: Sleep on it (postpone a decision)
body: A fixed phrase: wait a night before answering so you can think it over. (отложить решение до утра)
examples: Sleep on it and tell me tomorrow.
They slept on the offer and countered Monday.
We have slept on worse decisions than this one.

senses.head: Sleep with (have sex with)
body: A polite euphemism that fools nobody. Sleep together is the reciprocal form. (спать с кем-либо)
examples: Everyone assumed they had slept together.
She slept with his best friend and told him herself.
Half the plot turns on who sleeps with whom.

senses.head: Sleep off (recover by sleeping)
body: Of jet lag, a hangover, or a long flight; the object goes between the verb and the particle when it is a pronoun. (отоспаться после чего-либо)
examples: Sleep it off and call me in the morning.
He slept off the jet lag on the couch.
She has slept off worse hangovers than that.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: ✗ sleeped is not a form. Do not let slept /slɛpt/ slide into slipped /slɪpt/, the past of slip — the vowel is the only thing between them. In its ordinary sense sleep takes no object (I slept badly, ✗ I slept a bad night), though a house can sleep six.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it names an ongoing activity and takes the progressive freely (the baby is sleeping). The capacity sense (the cabin sleeps six) is stative and resists it: ✗ the cabin is sleeping six.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the ordinary sense, with no object: I slept badly, ✗ I slept a bad night. Transitive only in the capacity sense, where the object is a number of people: the cabin sleeps six.
entries.passive: no — ✗ six are slept by the cabin, and the ordinary sense has no object at all. The particle verbs do passivize: the offer was slept on and countered Monday; the jet lag was slept off on the couch.
entries.phrasal verbs: sleep around · sleep in · sleep off · sleep on · sleep over · sleep through · sleep with

entries.meaning: To clean a floor with a broom, or to move something (or move yourself) in a broad, forceful arc.
examples: I sweep the porch every Saturday.
He swept the broken glass into a dustpan.
Nobody has swept the shop floor in a week.
Sweep the crumbs onto a plate.
She swept the papers off the desk into a box.
Wind had swept the leaves into one corner of the yard.
A cold front sweeps down the valley every March.
The fire swept through the canyon in an afternoon.
Rumors have swept the office all week.
She sweeps into a room like she owns it.
He swept past the receptionist without a word.
They have swept out of two meetings this month.
No one expected them to sweep the series.
Their film swept the technical categories.
The team has swept all four games.
Searchlights sweep the fence line every few minutes.
Security swept the room for bugs.
Crews have swept both floors twice.
He sweeps aside every objection.
The complaint got swept under the rug.
They have swept two investigations under the rug.

senses.head: Clean with a broom
body: The literal sense. Americans sweep up a room; the verb upsweep is not used for cleaning. (мести, подметать)
examples: I sweep the porch every Saturday.
He swept the broken glass into a dustpan.
Nobody has swept the shop floor in a week.

senses.head: Push or clear away in one motion
body: One broad arm movement that clears a surface, with no broom involved. (смахнуть, смести)
examples: Sweep the crumbs onto a plate.
She swept the papers off the desk into a box.
Wind had swept the leaves into one corner of the yard.

senses.head: Move powerfully across a place
body: Of fire, storms, disease, rumor, or a political movement covering everything in its path. (пронестись, охватить)
examples: A cold front sweeps down the valley every March.
The fire swept through the canyon in an afternoon.
Rumors have swept the office all week.

senses.head: Move with grand, unhurried motion
body: Of a person entering or leaving a room. Slightly literary and often ironic. (величественно двигаться, шествовать)
examples: She sweeps into a room like she owns it.
He swept past the receptionist without a word.
They have swept out of two meetings this month.

senses.head: Win everything
body: American sports and awards usage: take every game in a series or every category on the night. (выиграть всухую, взять все награды)
examples: No one expected them to sweep the series.
Their film swept the technical categories.
The team has swept all four games.

senses.head: Search or scan systematically
body: Of security teams, searchlights, and radar: covering an area in a steady pattern. (прочесать, обследовать)
examples: Searchlights sweep the fence line every few minutes.
Security swept the room for bugs.
Crews have swept both floors twice.

senses.head: Sweep under the rug, sweep aside
body: Fixed phrases for hiding something embarrassing or brushing off an objection. (замять; отмахнуться)
examples: He sweeps aside every objection.
The complaint got swept under the rug.
They have swept two investigations under the rug.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary for sweeping a floor and for a team sweeping a series
