entries.contrast: ✗ sweeped is not standard, in any sense of the word. The same irregular past covers the figurative uses too: a fire swept through the canyon, a team swept the series.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, literal (sweep the porch) and figurative (the fire swept through the canyon, their film swept the technical categories).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in swept the broken glass into a dustpan, swept the series, swept the room for bugs; intransitive with a path phrase in the movement senses: she sweeps into a room, a cold front sweeps down the valley.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the room was swept for bugs; the complaint got swept under the rug; the shop floor has not been swept in a week. No passive of the movement sense: ✗ the canyon was swept through by the fire.
entries.phrasal verbs: sweep aside · sweep away · sweep up

entries.meaning: To give someone knowledge or a skill.
examples: Can you teach a beginner in a month?
She taught me algebra in one weekend.
He has taught himself three languages.
I teach two sections of writing in the fall.
She taught fourth grade for thirty years.
They had taught the course together before the merger.
One bad winter teaches you to keep chains in the trunk.
The recall taught the company nothing.
That experience has taught me to read the contract first.
That fine will teach him a lesson.
She taught them a lesson they still talk about.
Two audits have taught the department to file on time.

senses.head: Instruct someone in something
body: English splits what Russian учить covers with one verb: the teacher teaches and the student learns, so she learned me algebra is wrong. (учить, обучать кого-либо)
examples: Can you teach a beginner in a month?
She taught me algebra in one weekend.
He has taught himself three languages.

senses.head: Work as a teacher
body: With a subject, a grade, or a place, and often with no object at all: she teaches. (преподавать)
examples: I teach two sections of writing in the fall.
She taught fourth grade for thirty years.
They had taught the course together before the merger.

senses.head: Cause someone to learn from experience
body: The subject is an event or an experience rather than a person. (научить (об опыте, событии))
examples: One bad winter teaches you to keep chains in the trunk.
The recall taught the company nothing.
That experience has taught me to read the contract first.

senses.head: Teach someone a lesson
body: Informal and punitive: a threat or a boast about punishment, not real instruction. (проучить кого-либо)
examples: That fine will teach him a lesson.
She taught them a lesson they still talk about.
Two audits have taught the department to file on time.

entries.register: everyday — the ordinary verb for what a teacher does
entries.contrast: Taught and taut ("pulled tight") are homophones — /tɔt/ — and taught is also one letter from thought. English also splits what Russian учить covers with one verb: the teacher teaches, the student learns, so ✗ She learned me algebra is wrong for She taught me algebra.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the subject can be a person or an experience (that experience has taught me to read the contract first). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: ditransitive, and also both — two objects in she taught me algebra, one in she taught fourth grade, none at all in I teach. English splits the roles Russian учить covers: the teacher teaches, the student learns, so ✗ she learned me algebra.
entries.passive: yes, and either object can become the subject — I was taught algebra in one weekend; algebra is taught in the fall; the department has been taught to file on time.

entries.meaning: To use your mind to consider something, or to hold an opinion about it.
examples: I think we should wait a week.
She thought the meeting was on Thursday.
We had thought the issue was fixed.
Let me think.
He thought for a long moment before answering.
I have not thought clearly since four this morning.
Think about what you're asking her to do.
We thought about moving to Denver.
He has thought about applying for years.
I can't think of her last name.
She thought of three objections right away.
Nobody has thought of a better title.
I was thinking of leaving early.
We think we'll drive instead of flying.
They had thought they would be home by now.
Think it over and call me Monday.
She thought the whole plan through in one night.
They have thought this through more carefully than we have.
He thinks up a new excuse every week.
Who thought up this schedule?
They have thought up three names and hate all of them.
Her professors think highly of her.
We thought of him as a friend.
The industry has always thought of the company as a follower.
Think twice before you sign that.
He thought better of it and stayed home.
She has never thought twice about telling the truth.

senses.head: Hold an opinion, believe
body: The commonest use, normally with a that clause. In the negative, English moves the not onto think: I don't think he's coming. (думать, считать, полагать)
examples: I think we should wait a week.
She thought the meeting was on Thursday.
We had thought the issue was fixed.

senses.head: Use the mind, reason
body: No object: the activity itself. This is the sense in let me think and think straight. (думать, мыслить, соображать)
examples: Let me think.
He thought for a long moment before answering.
I have not thought clearly since four this morning.

senses.head: Think about (consider)
body: Turning something over in your mind, often over a long period. (думать о, обдумывать)
examples: Think about what you're asking her to do.
We thought about moving to Denver.
He has thought about applying for years.

senses.head: Think of (recall or come up with)
body: Retrieving a name or producing an idea on the spot. Often negative: I can't think of his name. (вспомнить; придумать)
examples: I can't think of her last name.
She thought of three objections right away.
Nobody has thought of a better title.

senses.head: Intend, be considering
body: Usually in the progressive, be thinking of plus an -ing form, which makes a plan sound tentative. (подумывать, собираться)
examples: I was thinking of leaving early.
We think we'll drive instead of flying.
They had thought they would be home by now.

senses.head: Think through, think over
body: Think through means follow the consequences all the way; think over means take time before answering. (обдумать до конца, взвесить)
examples: Think it over and call me Monday.
She thought the whole plan through in one night.
They have thought this through more carefully than we have.

senses.head: Think up (invent)
body: Of a name, an excuse, or a scheme, with a hint that it was made up quickly. (выдумать, придумать)
examples: He thinks up a new excuse every week.
Who thought up this schedule?
They have thought up three names and hate all of them.

senses.head: Think of as, think highly of
body: How you rate someone or what category you put them in. (относиться как к, быть высокого мнения)
examples: Her professors think highly of her.
We thought of him as a friend.
The industry has always thought of the company as a follower.

senses.head: Think twice, think better of
body: Fixed phrases: think twice warns before the act, think better of it reports a change of mind after it. (подумать дважды; передумать)
examples: Think twice before you sign that.
He thought better of it and stayed home.
She has never thought twice about telling the truth.

entries.register: everyday — among the most frequent verbs in English
entries.contrast: Other -ink verbs change the vowel — drink/drank/drunk, sink/sank/sunk — but think goes to -ought instead: ✗ thank is a different word entirely, and ✗ thunk is a joke. Thought is also a common noun (a passing thought).
entries.verb type: stative in the belief sense (I think we should wait), where the progressive is out: ✗ I am thinking he's wrong. Action in the reasoning sense, where it is normal: let me think, I was thinking of leaving early.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the reasoning sense (he thought for a long moment), transitive with a that-clause (I think we should wait) or a concrete object (think it over, thought up three names), and prepositional in think about / think of.
entries.passive: restricted — natural with a concrete object: this has been thought through more carefully than we did it; three names were thought up and all rejected. The belief sense passivizes only impersonally (it is thought that the two are related) — never personally: ✗ the meeting was thought on Thursday by her.
entries.phrasal verbs: think about, think of · think back · think of · think out · think over · think through · think up

entries.meaning: To sweep or curve something upward; you will meet it mostly as the participle upswept.
examples: The stylist can upsweep your hair for the ceremony.
She upswept her hair and pinned it with a tortoiseshell comb.
By seven she had upswept every loose strand.
That silhouette upsweeps sharply at the shoulder.
The designers have upswept the tail fins on the new model.
Wind has upswept the snow into a ridge along the roofline.

senses.head: Arrange hair upward
body: Rare as a verb; the adjective upswept and the noun an upsweep are far more common. For cleaning a room Americans say sweep up, never upsweep. (зачесать наверх, сделать высокую причёску)
examples: The stylist can upsweep your hair for the ceremony.
She upswept her hair and pinned it with a tortoiseshell comb.
By seven she had upswept every loose strand.

senses.head: Curve upward
body: Design and engineering vocabulary: upswept wingtips, upswept tail fins, an upswept shoulder line. (изгибать вверх, поднимать кверху)
examples: That silhouette upsweeps sharply at the shoulder.
The designers have upswept the tail fins on the new model.
Wind has upswept the snow into a ridge along the roofline.

entries.register: rare — met almost only as the adjective upswept; for cleaning, Americans say sweep up
entries.contrast: Rare as a verb, and it does not mean cleaning a room. For that, Americans say sweep up: I swept up the kitchen. You will meet this word almost only as the participle used as an adjective — upswept hair, upswept wingtips — or as the noun /ˈʌpswip/ for a hairstyle. It follows sweep.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but rare as a finite verb; you meet it mainly as the participle upswept used as an adjective (upswept hair, upswept wingtips).
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — the stylist can upsweep your hair, the designers have upswept the tail fins. It never means cleaning a room: Americans say sweep up, ✗ upsweep the kitchen.
entries.passive: yes — the tail fins have been upswept on the new model; her hair was upswept and pinned. In practice the same participle is far more often a plain adjective than a real passive.

entries.meaning: To cry, especially quietly and from deep feeling; literary in American English.
examples: Some people weep at weddings and some at airports.
She wept when she read the letter.
He has wept only twice in his adult life.
The old radiator weeps a little onto the floor.
The cut wept for two days.
That valve has wept since the day they installed it.
Nobody is going to weep for a bank.
The whole family wept through the service.
Historians have wept over the loss of that archive for two centuries.

senses.head: Cry from deep feeling
body: Literary. In everyday American English people cry; weep raises the register or the seriousness. (плакать, рыдать)
examples: Some people weep at weddings and some at airports.
She wept when she read the letter.
He has wept only twice in his adult life.

senses.head: Ooze liquid slowly
body: Of a wound, a pipe, a joint, or a valve losing liquid a drop at a time. Same irregular past. (сочиться, подтекать)
examples: The old radiator weeps a little onto the floor.
The cut wept for two days.
That valve has wept since the day they installed it.

senses.head: Weep for, weep over (mourn)
body: Formal, with for or over, and often ironic in the negative: nobody will weep for a bank. (оплакивать, скорбеть о)
examples: Nobody is going to weep for a bank.
The whole family wept through the service.
Historians have wept over the loss of that archive for two centuries.

entries.register: formal — literary and journalistic; in ordinary speech Americans cry
entries.contrast: Literary — in everyday American English people cry. The same verb also describes something that leaks slowly, with the same past: the pipe wept all night.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and literary in American English, where ordinary speech says cry. The leaking sense (the old radiator weeps) is equally dynamic.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every sense — no object: ✗ she wept the letter. What is mourned takes for or over: nobody is going to weep for a bank; historians have wept over the loss of that archive.
entries.passive: no — nothing to promote: ✗ the letter was wept by her. The prepositional passive exists but is literary and rare: a loss much wept over.

entries.meaning: To cause a great deal of damage or trouble; in practice almost always wreak havoc.
examples: A late frost can wreak havoc on the orchards.
The hurricane wreaked damage along sixty miles of coast.
Budget cuts have wreaked havoc on the department.
He wreaked his revenge slowly and in public.
The gods had wreaked their anger on the city.
No rival has wreaked vengeance that publicly in years.

senses.head: Wreak havoc, wreak damage
body: The modern past is wreaked. Wrought is historically the past of work, not of wreak, so American English writes wreaked havoc. (сеять хаос, причинять разрушения)
examples: A late frost can wreak havoc on the orchards.
The hurricane wreaked damage along sixty miles of coast.
Budget cuts have wreaked havoc on the department.

senses.head: Wreak vengeance
body: Formal and literary. The object is revenge, vengeance, or someone's anger, and it falls on or upon a target. (вершить месть, обрушить гнев)
examples: He wreaked his revenge slowly and in public.
The gods had wreaked their anger on the city.
No rival has wreaked vengeance that publicly in years.

entries.register: rare — outside the fixed phrase wreak havoc it barely appears
entries.contrast: The trap here is the spreadsheet's own form. Wrought is historically the past of work, not of wreak, and it survives only in fixed phrases — wrought iron, finely wrought, what hath God wrought. Modern American English writes wreaked havoc, not ✗ wrought havoc. The w is silent and the vowel is long: wreak is /rik/ like reek, ✗ not /rɛk/ like wreck.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and in modern American English almost frozen inside wreak havoc. Note that the past is wreaked, not ✗ wrought, which historically belongs to work.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory and nearly fixed — havoc, damage, vengeance, revenge: a late frost can wreak havoc on the orchards, ✗ a late frost can wreak. The target follows with on or upon.
entries.passive: restricted — havoc was wreaked along sixty miles of coast is grammatical but stiff; the idiom strongly prefers the active. Vengeance was wreaked upon the city survives only in the literary register.
